title: Superlinear randomized query lower bounds for submodular minimization
formal: Let \(R(n)\) be the minimum worst-case number of value-oracle queries needed by a randomized algorithm to find an exact minimizer of every real-valued submodular function on \(n\) elements, with success probability at least \(2/3\). Is \(R(n)=\omega(n)\), meaning \(R(n)/n\to\infty\) as \(n\to\infty\)?

source_formulation.text: We leave proving a super-linear lower bound on the query complexity of randomized algorithms for SFM as an open question.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 5

why: Submodular minimization is a central tractable optimization problem, yet its information requirements remain far from its best general algorithms. A superlinear randomized lower bound would establish that even unlimited computation and adaptive random querying cannot reduce exact minimization to a linear amount of oracle information.
status_note: The 2022 source explicitly leaves superlinear randomized query lower bounds open and explains why its deterministic argument does not transfer. No matching resolution for the bounded-query exact-minimization model was located in the bounded September 2026 check.

importance.reason: A fundamental information lower-bound gap for general submodular minimization, separating randomization from the first known superlinear deterministic obstruction.

sentences: A value oracle answers exact evaluations of an unknown submodular set function.
The randomized algorithm must find a true global minimizer on every input with constant success probability.
The question asks whether the worst-case query requirement grows faster than every constant multiple of the ground-set size.
Neither numeric evaluation cost nor local computation is charged.
Known deterministic and parallel-round lower bounds do not settle this randomized total-query question.

definitions: The ground set is \([n]\), and a function \(F:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\) is submodular if \(F(A)+F(B)\geq F(A\cup B)+F(A\cap B)\) for all subsets \(A,B\). No monotonicity, nonnegativity, symmetry or normalization is promised. A query specifies any subset \(S\) and receives its exact real value \(F(S)\). The algorithm may adapt later queries to all previous values and its own random choices. Its final answer is a subset \(S_*\) satisfying \(F(S_*)\leq F(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq[n]\); any minimizer is acceptable, including the empty or full set. For every fixed valid oracle \(F\), the probability of a correct output is at least \(2/3\). In the definition of \(R(n)\), a cost bound \(q\) requires at most \(q\) oracle calls on every input and every outcome of the random choices, not just in expectation. Arbitrary finite local computation and exact operations on the oracle answers are free. The algorithm has no direct access to a formula, table or circuit for \(F\). We use classical randomized query complexity: for each dimension, random coins select a deterministic adaptive query procedure, independently of \(F\); the maps and distributions must define measurable success events. An algorithm may depend on \(n\), so lower bounds also apply to nonuniform choices. The value magnitudes and their bit encodings do not enter the query cost. Exhaustively querying all \(2^n\) subsets shows that \(R(n)\) is finite. A superlinear lower bound means that for each real constant \(C>0\), all sufficiently large \(n\) satisfy \(R(n)>Cn\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked superlinear lower bound in the specified randomized bounded-query model. Alternatively prove the negation of that growth statement: a fixed constant C and infinitely many dimensions admit correct algorithms using at most Cn queries. An O(n)-query algorithm for all dimensions would suffice for a negative answer but is stronger than the logical negation. A deterministic lower bound, a lower bound on parallel rounds, or hardness only for finding a nonempty proper minimizer does not establish the target.

context_blocks.text: The source proves an Ω(n log n) deterministic query lower bound and explicitly asks for a superlinear randomized one. The selected target is any unbounded multiplicative improvement over n, rather than a demand for the same n log n expression.

In the deterministic construction, an adversary can exploit the algorithm’s fixed queries to delay discovery of a hidden set. The paper explains why random subsets can defeat the local obstruction used for that logarithmic factor. Transferring the deterministic proof without a new randomized argument is therefore insufficient.

The paper also proves a nearly linear lower bound on the number of adaptive parallel rounds when each round permits polynomially many queries. This measures how often answers must be used to choose the next batch. It does not imply a superlinear lower bound on the total number of sequentially adaptive queries.

Earlier lower bounds include a linear bound for general minimization and stronger statements for nontrivial minimizers of certain function classes. The requirement to exclude the empty and full sets changes the optimization problem; this card allows both and asks for the usual unconstrained minimum.

Exact oracle values can reveal more than comparisons between candidate subsets. A lower bound in this model must survive that extra information and cannot assume a bounded numeric range unless it constructs hard functions within that range. Conversely, bit complexity of evaluating an oracle is outside the target.

Strongly polynomial query upper bounds do not depend on the range of function values. The source compares algorithms with different amounts of local computation, including exponential local time; the lower-bound target here deliberately imposes no polynomial-time restriction.
